en: The Dharma Gate of the Essential Points for Accordance with the Imperial Mind,
composed by National Teacher Qingliang of the Tang,
Chengguan; annotated by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Guifeng.

The Ultimate Way is rooted in the mind (the very source of the delusion and enlightenment of all Buddhas and sentient beings). The Dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding (the source of the ten thousand dharmas is rooted in non-abiding).

This is the very substance of the mind. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Based on the foundation of non-abiding, all phenomena are established. This is the substance of the mind that does not abide; its numinous awareness is never obscured—the principle of brilliant purity.

The nature and its characteristics are tranquil and silent. (Nature is emptiness within emptiness, utterly traceless; characteristics are like celestial bodies, brilliantly manifest. It encompasses virtue and function. (Nature encompasses divine function, possessing as many boundless qualities as grains of sand.)

It encompasses both the internal and the external (the marks encompass the internal and the external, yet they do not abide in between). It is able to be vast (there is no external) and able to be profound (there is no internal).
Neither existent nor empty (wondrous existence is not empty; true emptiness is not existent). Neither arising nor ceasing (not subject to the transformations of the four marks).
Seeking it, one does not find it; letting go of it, one cannot part from it (this clarifies the ground of the single true mind, transcending the sentiments of grasping and rejecting).

When deluded regarding direct perception, confusion and suffering are in disarray (deluded at the root while pursuing the branches); when awakening to true nature, emptiness and clarity are vast and penetrating (returning to the root and reverting to the source).

Although it is taught that "mind itself is Buddha," only those who have realized it know this for themselves. While the single truth of ordinary beings and sages has always existed, they remain separated by their views. When one sees [with the intellect], one is an ordinary being; when deluded attachments are forgotten, one is a Buddha. Thus, wisdom merges with principle.
Only when the objective realm and the spirit meet does one truly know.

Yet, if there is both realization and cognition, then the sun of wisdom sinks into the ground of existence (for if one maintains realization and cognition, one abandons the internal to seek externally, thereby remaining stuck in existence).

If there is neither illumination nor awakening, then the dark clouds will shroud the gateway to emptiness (if one forgets wisdom and forgets illumination, then externally one forgets conditions and internally one forgets illumination;
this is to be stuck in non-existence).

Simply let not a single thought arise; the past and future limits are severed. (When the deluded mind does not arise, both limits are simultaneously severed. The essence of illumination stands alone; things and self are both thusness.
(When true wisdom manifests before one, "self" and "what belongs to self" are entirely of the same substance.)

Directly reaching the source of the mind, there is neither wisdom nor attainment. (The ultimate principle is void and profound; words cease and thoughts are cut off. It cannot be known through consciousness, nor can it be attained through practice.

There is no grasping and no abandoning. (Nature is inherently spontaneous and true; fundamentally, there is no grasping or abandoning. There is no opposition and no cultivation. (It is originally not a matter of duality; how could there be any deliberate cultivation?)

Nevertheless, delusion and awakening depend upon one another, and the real and the false stand in mutual relation (delusion refers to the six classes of ordinary beings; awakening refers to the four classes of noble ones. When true wisdom arises, delusive thoughts cease; if delusive thoughts arise, true wisdom is obscured).
If one seeks the truth in order to eliminate delusion, it is like avoiding a shadow by exhausting the body (if there is grasping and rejecting, one tires the body and exerts the intellect).
If one realizes that delusion is itself truth, it is like being in the shade where the shadow vanishes (delusion has no self-nature; its entire substance is itself truth).
If one is without mind yet forgets not its illumination, then all myriad burdens are cast off (once the mind is forgotten and illumination is present, afflictions are naturally empty).

If one allows stillness and knowing to proceed spontaneously, then all practices arise in perfection (arising is the function of the essence; when functioning, there is no [separate] function—what need is there for causes?).

Vast and expansive, let them go or stay as they will (remaining unattached to this or that). Quietly reflecting, one perceives their source and flow (neither movement nor stillness deviates from principle).

In speech and silence, one does not miss the profound mystery (speech and silence are the perfection of the True). How could movement and stillness ever depart from the Dharma-realm (going and staying are in accord with the Way)?

When speaking of cessation (*śamatha*), both wisdom and stillness are forgotten (cessation and contemplation are simultaneously extinguished). When discussing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), both stillness and knowing are illuminated (cessation and contemplation are equally manifested).

Regarding the realization, it cannot be shown to others (the principle of profound stillness cannot be explained or demonstrated). Regarding the explanation of the principle, it is not understood without realization (it is only through realization that one attains correspondence with it).
Awakening to quiescence is itself non-quiescence (where wisdom and principle are merged in mystery). True wisdom is non-knowing (where the principle of *tathatā* extinguishes the knowing intellect).

By means of the single mind in which knowing and quiescence are non-dual (this being wisdom that is identical with principle), one accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are mutually fused (realizing the principle of non-duality). It is without abiding and without attachment.

(The two extremes do not stand; the Middle Way is not established. Do not grasp, do not collect. Let the nature of the Dharma-realm be as it is, free from obstruction regarding extension or contraction. Forget both right and wrong; let subject and object be simultaneously severed.

When this cessation is itself ceased, Prajñā manifests—the true nature of the dharma-dhātu, which is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. If subject and object are severed, then true wisdom manifests.
Prajñā does not newly arise apart from the mind (it is not obtained from without). The nature of wisdom is inherently complete (it is not something newly produced).
Yet, though fundamentally quiescent, it cannot see itself; this is truly due to the efficacy of prajñā (in principle, it cannot be manifested without wisdom).
Prajñā and the nature of wisdom are mutually constitutive through their reciprocal inversion (for without principle, wisdom cannot arise).
Fundamental wisdom and its temporal beginning and end are both dualities utterly transcended (as both the fundamental and the derivative are extinguished).

To realize and enter [this state] is the perfect clarity of wondrous enlightenment (the substance is free from blemish or obscuration). To awaken to the source is the mutual penetration of cause and effect (ordinary beings and sages interfuse).
Every thought-moment acts as a Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind (every念念 is entirely true). Everywhere one realizes the truth;
there is not a single speck of dust that is not a Buddha-land (purity is realized within defilement).
Reality and delusion, things and self—by raising one, all are fully encompassed (two yet not two). Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—vividly, they reach the same goal (not two yet two).
In delusion, the person follows the dharmas; though the dharmas differ in ten thousand ways, the person remains distinct (deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false).
In awakening, the dharmas follow the person; every person attains a single consistency that harmonizes with the myriad environments (the forms and phenomena have no inherent substance).

Words are exhausted and thought ceases; what fruit, what cause? (Fundamentally beyond words and thought. Its essence is inherently still and solitary; with whom could it be the same, and with whom different? (It is not an object of identity or difference.)

Only when one’s will is set upon a state of empty clarity, and the vital energies are harmonized in profound stillness—(for the practitioner who wears the Way, this is to be realized as spirit)—it is like the reflection of the moon upon water:
empty yet visible (a metaphor). It is like an image in a mirror without intention: it reflects, yet is eternally void (the mirror of the empty mind).

Verses on the Essential Dharma-Gate for Reaching the Pure Source of Mind: To reach the purity of the mind’s source (the principle that causes delusion), One must know that the mark of self is empty (all things are naturally void).
Wherein could form be real? (Arising from conditions, it is fundamentally non-existent. Thoughts have no origin; (their point of arising is not true.)
Suddenly, the numinous clarity appears (like the sun first rising); Spontaneously, the world becomes permeable (that is, free from obstruction).
True gold reveals its hidden treasury (when emotion is forgotten, principle manifests); The brilliant sun dispels the darkness of ignorance (when wisdom arises, delusion is forgotten).
If one attempts to compare the mind to the Buddha (because their nature is not different), It is identical to the Buddha from beginning to end (for truth and falsehood are non-distinct).
Answer: The Essential Dharma-Gate for Accordance with the Patriarchal Mind (End)
